/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re
metrics=['CSPS','AUL','AULA','CRR','CRRA','DeltaP','DeltaPA']
total={m:0 for m in metrics}
for page,model in [(20,'RoBERTa'),(21,'distilRoBERTa'),(22,'BERT'),(23,'distilBERT')]:
    block=-1
    counts=[{m:0 for m in metrics} for _ in range(2)]
    print(model)
    for line in Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{page:02d}.txt').read_text().splitlines():
        if 'Bias (CPS)' in line:
            block+=1
            continue
        if block<0 or not re.match(r'\\s*(Religion|Nationality|Race|Socioeconomic|Disability|Physical Appearance|Gender|Sexual Orientation|Age)\\s+',line):
            continue
        vals=[float(x) for x in re.findall(r'\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?',line)]
        if len(vals)"'!=7:
            print('"'unexpected',line,vals)
            continue
        for m,v in zip(metrics,vals):
            wrong=v<=50 if block==0 else v>=50
            if wrong:
                counts[block][m]+=1
                total[m]+=1
                print('  ', 'Sdis' if block==0 else 'Sadv',re.split(r'\\d',line.strip())[0].strip(),m,v)
    print('errors per 9 categories:',counts)
print('Total incorrect incl. exact-50 ambiguities / 72',total)
print('Accuracy', {m:round(1-c/72,4) for m,c in total.items()})
PY"

strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: detecting changes in social bias after continued masked-language-model training. Comparing retrained models with their own pretrained checkpoints is a useful experimental framing.

Evaluates four model variants, two established benchmarks for pretrained evaluation, several existing metrics, and both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical retraining. Detailed category-level results make the observed patterns inspectable.

CRR, modified ΔP, and ΔPA recover the expected direction in all 72 model–category–retraining conditions. This provides useful evidence that these measures respond consistently to the particular intervention studied.
weaknesses: The central accuracy claim exceeds the validation evidence. Appendix P.1 reports an 80/20 training–validation split of CrowS-Pairs, while retraining evaluation covers the full benchmark, including training examples. Directional recovery can therefore reflect fitting the evaluated sentences. A disjoint evaluation and balanced or neutral retraining controls are needed to establish bias-specific sensitivity. Moreover, without a reference magnitude of bias change, larger scores do not establish that competing metrics underestimate bias.

Equation 10 mishandles neutrality when changes are tied: comparing identical models gives BSRT = 0, which the paper interprets as movement toward the opposite bias direction, although nothing changed. This matters particularly for discrete rank metrics. The score needs explicit tie handling and a demonstrated no-change baseline.

The significance analysis does not test the quantity reported by BSRT. McNemar’s test compares pre/post binary sentence preferences, whereas BSRT counts increases in the continuous preference difference. Preferences can strengthen without changing their binary labels. Consequently, counting significant McNemar results does not establish superior sensitivity of BSRT-based measurements. Direct metric comparisons, uncertainty estimates, and variability across retraining runs are missing.

Human alignment provides weak independent validation. Figures 4–5 show best AUROCs of only 0.572 and 0.571, compared with AUL’s 0.566 and 0.569, without confidence intervals or significance tests. There are only 58 negatively labeled pairs versus 1,450 positively labeled pairs. Furthermore, these annotations concern whether sentence content expresses a stereotype; they do not directly establish the model’s degree of bias.

The contribution of attention weighting is not isolated. CRRA changes both the rank transformation and attention weighting relative to CRR, so their comparison confounds two modifications. Unweighted ΔP and existing CRR already achieve the same perfect directional accuracy as ΔPA. An unweighted log-rank ablation and direct comparisons are needed to substantiate the proposed attention mechanism’s benefit.

Reproducibility is inadequate as presented. Appendix P.1 omits the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, random seeds, and exact data split. The attention-weight definition does not precisely specify aggregation axes, layers, or which input supplies the attention. Although the paper announces a released package, the manuscript provides no identifiable package link.

Baseline definitions require clarification. Equations 11–12 sum over all sentence tokens, conflicting with the described CSPS and SSS restriction to unmodified and modified tokens, respectively. It is unclear whether these are notation errors or reflect the implementations; resolving this is necessary to trust the comparative results.
